# Batcave Bitflips

Category: Reversing | Difficulty: Medium | Flag: `UMASS{__p4tche5_0n_p4tche$__#}`

## TL;DR

A license-checker binary that's been "hit by cosmic rays" (intentional bitflips). The decryption routine has an `OR` where there should be an `XOR`, meaning the flag is simply `FLAG_data XOR EXPECTED_hash` — no hash reversal or license key brute-force needed.

## What We're Given

A single ELF binary: `batcave_license_checker`. The flavor text is doing some real work here:

> "Batman's AI agent deleted source code. Old debug version hit by cosmic rays (bitflips)."

That last sentence is the whole challenge. "Bitflips" isn't just a cool name — it's telling us the binary has been deliberately corrupted at the bit level. Our job is to figure out what got flipped and what that means for getting the flag.

## Initial Recon

Standard first moves: `file` and `checksec` to understand what we're dealing with.
    
    `$ file batcave_license_checker
    batcave_license_checker: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, dynamically linked, not stripped

The core technique: When you see a "bitflip" challenge, the binary is intentionally broken. Map out every function and look for instructions that are almost right but slightly off — wrong shift amounts, OR vs XOR, off-by-one constants. The bug is usually one bit away from correct behavior.

The clever shortcut: Instead of fixing all the bitflips and reversing the hash, we reasoned backward from the goal. We asked: "what would the decryption do if it were correct, and what values would flow through it?" That led directly to `FLAG ^ EXPECTED = plaintext`.

Pattern to remember: Anytime a CTF binary XORs encrypted data against a hash value, and you can extract both the encrypted data and the expected hash from the binary, you can skip the whole hash computation. The expected hash is the key.

Tools used:

  * Binary Ninja for static analysis and decompilation
  * Python for the one-liner XOR

The intended path (which we skipped entirely) was probably: identify all three bitflips, patch the binary to fix them, figure out that `!_batman-robin-alfred_((67||67))` is the license key, run the fixed binary, get the flag. Our path took about 5 minutes. Respect to anyone who did it the hard way though — it's a clean challenge design.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Challenges

## Music Theory (Fwn)

Given mp4 file and as you can see there is a text underneath of the video. And it seems like it is base64 encoded format:

Using CyberChef, the data was decoded from Base64 format. The provided clue indicated that this artifact used steganography in conjunction with TrueCrypt.

### What is truecrypt?

TrueCrypt is an open-source software used for on-the-fly encryption (OTFE). It creates a virtual encrypted disk within a file and can also encrypt a partition or an entire storage device.

To access the encrypted data, the volume must be mounted by entering the correct passphrase, after which the contents become available.

Since TrueCrypt has been discontinued, VeraCrypt, which provides the same functionality, is used instead.

### Recon

After inspecting the file, I we found that the comment field contained something interesting. I used ExifTool to extract metadata from the video file.

`
    
    1
    

 | 
    
    └─$ exiftool enterscoretitlehere.mp4
    

`

The string `6b65796f66636d616a6f72` appears to be in hexadecimal format. When converted to ASCII text, it translates to `keyofcmajor`

This finding may serve as the password required to decrypt the encrypted mounted disk.

### Extracting

Now for the fun part. Open VeraCrypt and choose any available drive letter (A, B, C, or any other). Then, enter the provided password to mount the volume. Once mounted, you will be able to access the decrypted contents.

Once you be able to decrypt it,open the file and grab the flag!

## The Vulnerability / Trick

This challenge actually has two layers. Here's where it gets nasty (and satisfying).

### Layer 1: The l0l4 Chunks (Red Herring)

Concatenating all 64 `l0l4` chunk payloads produces a valid JPEG file. Here's what it contains:

That's the infamous "HATE" monologue from Harlan Ellison's I Have No Mouth, and I Must Scream — delivered by AM, a malevolent AI. Extremely on-brand for a CTF challenge, extremely not the flag.

The JPEG also has steghide data embedded in it. Running:
    
    steghide extract -sf combined_l0l4.jpg -p ""

...extracts `teeny.mp3`. It's a Rick Roll. A literal Rick Roll. We got got.

We then spent way too long analyzing this audio file. Spectrogram? Just music. Reversed? Still music. Slowed down? Music, but slower. DTMF, SSTV, Morse? Nothing.

The JPEG with the steghide Rick Roll is the "Chunk Splice" half of the challenge name. It's entirely a distraction. The challenge authors built a very convincing fake solve path. Respect and frustration in equal measure.

### Layer 2: BPCS in the Clean Image (The Real Thing)

This is where "BPCS" in the challenge name matters. Bit-Plane Complexity Segmentation (BPCS) is a steganography technique that hides data by replacing high-complexity regions of an image's bit planes with secret data. The key insight: human eyes (and most detectors) can't distinguish between a "naturally noisy" image region and one that's been replaced with arbitrary data — because both look like visual noise.

Here's how BPCS works at a high level:

  1. Take each color channel of an image and decompose it into 8 bit planes (one per bit, from MSB to LSB)
  2. Divide each bit plane into 8x8 blocks
  3. Measure each block's complexity — how many pixel transitions happen horizontally and vertically, divided by the maximum possible transitions for that block size (112 for 8x8)
  4. Blocks above an alpha threshold (here, `alpha=0.45`) are considered "complex" enough that swapping them with secret data won't be visually detectable
  5. Convert pixel values to CGC (Canonical Gray Code) first — this makes adjacent bit planes more coherent and gives you more complex regions to work with

The important twist: stripping the `l0l4` chunks from `lush.png` and comparing pixel values to the resulting image shows they're identical. PIL ignores unknown chunks during loading, so when you load `lush.png`, you already get the "clean" pixel data. The BPCS was applied to the image before the `l0l4` chunks were added.

This means the image contains two independent hidden layers:

  * In the chunks: fake JPEG red herring
  * In the pixel data itself: the actual flag, BPCS-embedded

We also spent time trying to do BPCS on the JPEG from the chunks, which produced garbage — because the JPEG wasn't the carrier, the PNG pixel data was.

### Attack Flow

Image: Attack_Flow

From our code analysis, we know the app accepts file uploads at `POST /submit`. The upload filter in `StoryController.java` only allows `text/plain` and `application/pdf`. But when the server serves files back, it uses `Files.probeContentType()`, which reads the file extension.

> The `Files.probeContentType()` method is used to identify the MIME type of a file.

We need one file that serves two purposes: setup (when the editorial bot runs it) and exfiltration (when the report-runner bot runs it). The same file is visited by both bots, so we detect which one we are by checking for the FLAG cookie.

Branch A: fires when there is NO FLAG cookie → we are the editorial bot → do all the setup work (actuator, CSRF, trigger report-runner).

Branch B: fires when FLAG cookie IS present → we are the report-runner bot → read `document.cookie` and send the flag out.

So, when we upload a file, we need to keep `Content-Type` as `text/plain`, as this is what passes the server’s filter.

# Pàlcam CyberGames 2026

## Éxito rotundo en la Pàlcam CyberGames 2026

La primera edición de las Pàlcam CyberGames 2026 ha superado todas las expectativas y se ha convertido en una experiencia de gran impacto dentro del ámbito de la ciberseguridad.

Tras 36 horas de competición intensa, el evento ha demostrado que el talento, la capacidad técnica y la pasión por la seguridad digital no tienen límites. También ha puesto en valor el enorme potencial de la plataforma SoterCTF, entorno en el que se ha desarrollado toda la competición.

Las cifras hablan por sí solas:

  * 377 participantes registrados
  * 302 equipos compitiendo simultáneamente
  * Participación de 16 países diferentes, entre ellos España, India, Marruecos o China
  * 27 retos únicos planteados durante la competición
  * El 100% de los retos resueltos, demostrando el altísimo nivel técnico de los participantes
  * Un total de 2.561 flags validadas

La lucha por el podio fue especialmente intensa: los tres primeros equipos empataron con 12.930 puntos, y la clasificación final se decidió por la velocidad de entrega.

Este gran éxito ha sido posible gracias a un grupo de alumnos de segundo curso de ASIX-CIBER, que orientaron su proyecto hacia su mayor pasión: la ciberseguridad.

Consiguieron transformar una actividad de clase en una competición de alto nivel, capaz de atraer participantes internacionales y de generar una experiencia real y exigente, muy cercana a los retos profesionales del sector.

Más allá de los resultados, esta iniciativa refleja perfectamente la manera de entender el aprendizaje en Pàlcam: conectar el aula con la realidad, potenciar el talento y dar espacio para que el alumnado pueda llevar sus ideas mucho más allá.

Felicidades a los equipos ganadores y, especialmente, a nuestros alumnos por haber hecho posible este proyecto.
